## Findings
HIGH — Exported weights lose their window recipe on republishing. scripts/t112/push_arm.py:107 saves only model, architecture, resolution and normalization.
The converter explicitly accepts already-converted weights at lines 73–79, but line 116 derives the clean flag only from recipe and defaults it to false.
Thus original clean checkpoint → first render true → exported checkpoint → second render false.
The architecture reviewer reproduced this with the exact metadata statements and an in-memory save stub.
This does not invalidate F's current first push from its original SWA.
Preserve the flag in exported metadata, read it on reimport, and test the round trip.

HIGH — Nearly empty masks bypass the clean contract and its warning. src/coat_data.py:378–380 and scripts/t112/build_t112_kernel.py:225–227 replace fewer than three real valid indices with synthetic [0,1,2] before checking clean eligibility.
Executing F's rendered _eval_centers with 44-slot masks containing zero, one (slot 5), or two (slots 5–6) valid entries returns centre 1 twelve times: 12/12 windows touch blanks, with no diagnostic.
The real dataset getitem also returns a bag for each case.
Consequently the shell's fallback count can report zero despite these invalid windows.
Keep the original validity set for clean selection;
refuse invalid training bags and announce any intentional serving fallback.
Hidden-test frequency is unknown;
this review does not claim these masks occurred in F training.
The separately logged fallback for at least three valid slots but no legal triplet is intentional in 8a25545, not a separate regression.
A control mask [0,11,12,21,22] correctly logs it in serving and raises in training.
MEDIUM — Legacy checkpoints cannot resume under their original rule. src/coat_train.py:115–125 defaults old normalization metadata but not the new window field.
The unconditional recipe comparison at lines 309–315 therefore sees (None, False) even with explicit --dirty-windows.
Default an absent historical field to false.

Running mean of the tail epochs' weights, updated in place.
Run 2's last five epochs scored 0.8727 / 0.8662 / 0.8740 / 0.8711 / 0.8674 -- a spread of 0.0078 against a +/-0.036 noise band on 58 studies.
They are statistically indistinguishable, so "save the argmax" is selecting on noise with the same 58 studies that are our only measuring instrument.
Averaging the tail is the standard answer precisely when the tail is equivalent, which we have now measured it to be.
Integer buffers (num_batches_tracked) take the latest value rather than a mean: they are counters, and a fractional counter is not a thing.
Note what this does not do: BatchNorm running statistics are averaged along with the weights rather than recomputed over the data.

They are already running means over the same distribution and the tail epochs sit close together, so this is the cheap approximation of update_bn -- which would cost another pass over the loader, and the loader is the bottleneck.
If the averaged checkpoint ever scores worse than the argmax one by more than noise, that approximation is the first thing to suspect.

Write the every-epoch continuation checkpoint, atomically.
Separate from --out on purpose.

--out is the argmax checkpoint and is written only on an improving epoch, so it is usually not the last epoch -- T004's was epoch 4 of 8 -- and resuming from it would silently restart the run four epochs early with no optimizer state.
This file is the last epoch, always, and carries the whole machine rather than the weights.
It is a strict superset of --out's keys, so every existing reader (compare_ckpts.py, the inference kernels, attn_divergence.py, gradcam.py) can be pointed at it unchanged.

Written to a temp file and os.replaced in: the process this file exists to survive is one that dies at an arbitrary moment, and a half-written checkpoint is worse than none because torch.load fails only at the end.

Restore a run from save_resume's file and return where it left off.
Loaded on the CPU whatever the venue: Optimizer.load_state_dict moves its own state onto each parameter's device, and the RNG states have to be CPU tensors anyway.
The argument check is the point of this function as much as the loading is.
--epochs sets the cosine schedule's horizon and which epochs are in the SWA tail;
--folds/--split-seed set which studies are held out;
--bs and --accum set how many optimizer steps an epoch is.
Continuing under a changed value produces a checkpoint no single run could have produced, and every downstream comparison in this project assumes otherwise.

A flag added to train.py after a checkpoint was written is simply absent from its args, and at its default that is not a recipe change: the interrupted run trained under code where the flag did not exist, which is the same thing as the flag being off.
Without this, adding any flag bricks every .last.pt on disk -- T062's and T050's, both listed as resumable -- and the failure would look like a recipe divergence rather than a code change.
An absent key whose value now differs from the default is still a diff and still fatal, which is the case that matters.
The argmax and SWA checkpoints belong to the interrupted run's --out, recorded in the checkpoint (not inferred from this file's name, which may be a copy).

If the continuation runs under a different --out and no resumed epoch improves on the restored best, nothing would be written to the new stem and the final reload-and-dump would fail on a missing file.
Carry them over, so the new stem describes the whole run.

The commit this run's code came from, and whether it was clean.
A Kaggle run's provenance is the code dataset's version note, which the 2026-08-21 ruling requires to name a commit.
A local run has no dataset, so the equivalent has to travel inside the checkpoint: a checkpoint on disk must be attributable without the log that announced it.
dirty is recorded rather than enforced -- refusing to train would turn a provenance rule into an availability problem, and the honest failure is a checkpoint that says it cannot be reproduced.
RUN FROM THE REPOSITORY ROOT, not from src/.

Git resolves a pathspec against the process CWD, so -- src/ scripts/ executed in <repo>/src meant <repo>/src/src/ and <repo>/src/scripts/ -- neither exists, git exits 0 with no output, and dirty was False on EVERY run ever recorded (measured 2026-09-19: git ls-files -- src/ returns 0 entries from src/ and 28 from the root).
git rev-parse HEAD is indifferent to the CWD, which is why the commit half looked like evidence that the whole thing worked.
It defeated exactly the case it was written for: a checkpoint written from an uncommitted tree claiming to be attributable.

root is a parameter so the invariant can be tested on a REAL throwaway repository -- pointed at the root it reports dirt, pointed at src/ it reports clean over the same dirty tree, which is the control that gives the check teeth.
Nothing passes it in production.

THE SEED IS PART OF THE RESULT, not part of the invocation.

The interval is a pair of order statistics over boot draws, so the same command on the same files gives a different band at a different seed: measured over seeds 0-4 on the T019 comparison the half-width spans 0.001913-0.002024, about 5%.
data/oof/README.md documents "band +/-0.0019" for a call that prints +/-0.0020 at the default seed -- seed 2 is the one that reproduces it, and nothing on the page said so.
Printing it costs nine characters and makes every archived band re-derivable;
the vocabulary every decision rule here is written in is "resolved", and an endpoint within that margin can flip on a re-run of the identical command.
hd == 0 means the two sides are the same predictions.
Worth saying plainly rather than dividing by it: this is what a sanity check of the harness looks like, and it used to raise ZeroDivisionError here.
The interval, not the point estimate, is the result.
An interval spanning zero means the files cannot tell these two checkpoints apart -- which is a finding, and specifically not a licence to fall back on preferring the mechanism.
That reasoning cost this project 0.008 once (run 3, T008).
Said out loud because the point of the block is the comparison the eye will not make on its own: one column's band is far wider than the mean's, so a per-label delta must clear a much higher bar.
Dropping the resamples where a column was degenerate is selection ON THE OUTCOME: for a rare column the excluded draws are exactly the extreme ones, so what survives is optimistically NARROW.
The count is printed per label above;
this says what a short count means, because these bands now decide column-level questions.
Make a hung run legible, before it hangs.
Two hangs (T004 epoch 8, T007 epoch 6) were diagnosed from /proc alone and neither could be located, for two separate reasons that both live here.
Line buffering. A redirected stdout is block-buffered, and SIGTERM does not flush it, so a killed run loses whatever is still in the buffer.

What made the logs look live was an accident: multiprocessing flushes the parent's streams before every fork, so the log advanced exactly three times an epoch, when the train, gold and corpus loaders built their workers.
The last line in a hung run's log is therefore the state at the previous loader, not at the hang -- which is why "hung at the start of epoch 6" could not be read off it.
Measured, not assumed (T007's hang_report section 1).

The traceback. faulthandler's handler is installed at the C level and does not need the GIL, so kill -USR1 <pid> dumps every thread's Python stack even while the main thread is spinning inside a C call -- the exact state both hangs were in, and the one where a Python-level handler would never have run.
scripts/gpu_watchdog.sh sends this before it kills.

- Do not run CPU-heavy analysis while a fold is training (measured 2026-08-26).
train.py uses --workers 8 and the dataloader saturates what is left of the 16 cores.
Two folds with identical 14.1 min/epoch train time came out very differently: T020, run while the session was mostly idle, took 125 min wall for 8 epochs (11 min overhead);
T004, run while smoke_test (436 checks), compare_ckpts bootstraps, label_gaps and attn_divergence were being run repeatedly, took 145 min for 7 epochs (46 min overhead) — about 24% slower.
Analysis is cheap and feels free;
it is not, and under the one-fold rule a slower run is a longer time at 87 °C.
Batch the reads, or do them in the cooldown gap.

Multi-fold work is a multi-day proposition locally — Kaggle's 30 h/week is the lane that does not touch the card at all. To queue work without violating this, use scripts/gpu_queue.sh job1.sh [job2.sh ...]: it starts each job only once the card is ≤55 °C and has been idle ≥20 min, runs exactly one job per entry, and logs the observed temperature and idle gap for every launch.
It decides occupancy from nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps, never a pgrep pattern — a watcher naming the pattern it waits for matches itself, which once deadlocked five shells here.
Rebuild from the checkpoint's own saved args, never from CLI flags.
train.py stores vars(args) in every checkpoint.

Reconstructing from that is the difference between an instrument and a guess: an --adjacent checkpoint fed non-adjacent channels, or a --per-label-attn one rebuilt with shared pooling, loads with a shape error if you are lucky and silently localizes the wrong thing if you are not.
The flags src/train.py actually accepts, read from its own --help.

Falling back rather than failing means a dataset push that forgot a file still trains something, and the log below says which targets were actually used.
The header manifest is an optimisation, never a requirement: without it every series is scanned live exactly as before, just slower.
So a kernel whose code dataset predates the manifest still trains.
T067: prefer the WIDER manifest.
manifest.csv covers the 13,221 series --seqs 1 opens;
manifest_all.csv covers all 24,371.

Under --seqs 2 the run opens 21,334 of them, so with the narrow file ~8,100 series would scan their headers live -- and on Kaggle's network mount ~63% of a series read is wait, not CPU, which is the expensive half of the run.

Preferring the superset is behaviour-neutral, verified 2026-09-08 rather than assumed: the two files have identical columns, manifest.csv is an exact subset, and the 13,221 shared rows disagree in ZERO cells.
On top of that SeriesPlan.matches re-guards every row against the files actually on disk, so a stale plan falls back to a live scan exactly as an absent row does.
The fallback chain keeps an older code dataset training.
The code dataset is versioned separately from this kernel, so it can be older than the flags this kernel wants to pass.

That has now cost two separate incidents -- T001 found the dataset predating P0-P2 entirely, and T009's first five fold launches all died on "unrecognized arguments: --folds". argparse fails loudly, but only after the kernel has queued, provisioned a GPU and imported torch.

it costs a second. split("=") because argparse accepts --flag=value, and this check reads the literal token: "--mirror=0.5" is not a substring of the helptext even when "--mirror" is, so the =-form made a current dataset look stale.
That cost a launch on 2026-08-27. scripts/push_family.py's own validator already split on "=", so the two disagreed and the local one passed what the kernel then rejected.
Keep them in agreement.
Exact flag tokens, not a in helptext.

A substring test false-PASSES on any prefix of a real flag -- "--mirr", "--rot", "--per-label" and "--epoch" all "pass" against a helptext containing --mirror/--rotate/ --per-label-attn/--epochs, and then argparse kills the run on Kaggle after the mount and the GPU provision.
That is precisely what this guard exists to prevent, and a truncated flag name is the likeliest way to trip it.
Same extraction as scripts/push_family.py::known_flags, deliberately: smoke_test pins the two to identical verdicts.

T004: one attention distribution per label, off by default.
Named test_t004_ on purpose.
Two sessions once both defined test_paired_comparison, Python kept one, the other's checks never ran, and the suite still reported success (PROGRESS.md).
The house rule: the flag off must be the model that scored LB 0.921.
The design claim: at init every label shares one distribution, so an untrained per-label model computes what shared attention computes.
Padding must be exactly zero for every label, in fp32 and under autocast.
Divergence must be reachable, or the flag buys nothing.
The inference kernels must rebuild the architecture from the checkpoint.

The round trip that would otherwise fail months from now: a checkpoint trained with the flag must rebuild from its own args alone, and every checkpoint trained BEFORE the flag existed must still load untouched -- the ten behind LB 0.921 have no per_label_attn key at all.
The confound a review caught on 2026-08-26: --per-label-attn also changed dropout from one shared mask to twelve independent ones, which is a second variable inside a one-variable experiment.
Pinned in BOTH directions so neither the default (T004's measured run) nor the control can drift.
